title: Press on (Philippians 3:12–21)
hook: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whole résumé moved into the loss column, and your line was all else is loss.

Watch the last fifty meters of a race. Nobody in the lead looks back. Coaches drill it: turn your head to see who's behind you, and you lose a step. The runners lean forward, chest out, reaching for a line on the ground. Paul has just told the Philippians that everything behind him is loss. Now he faces the other way, and reaches for the language of the stadium: a track, a line, a prize.

He starts with an admission. Paul, the great apostle, says he hasn't arrived. In the King James Bible: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended." Not yet. I haven't got hold of it. Then the famous lines: "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." Every phrase is a runner. Forgetting what's behind. Reaching forth, the body leaning out. The mark, the goal at the end of the track. The prize. The verb for press is worth a second look. In Greek it's a word for chasing, pursuing hard. A few verses earlier, Paul used the very same word about his past: he had been zealous, persecuting the church. The same energy that once hunted Christians now runs toward Christ. Paul doesn't become a calmer man. He points the same drive in a new direction. And forgetting isn't amnesia. He remembers his past well enough to write it down a few verses earlier. He means it no longer steers: not his old credentials, not his old wrongs. Then he widens the picture: "For our conversation is in heaven." You live here, he says, but your city is somewhere else. So you run.
screen: then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Think of something you keep replaying, a failure, an old win, a conversation you can't stop rewriting, and notice how much attention it still takes. Then gently turn your head the other way: what's one small thing in front of you that you've put off while you looked back, a call, a page, an apology, a first lap? Picture taking the first step toward it, just one, and if you pray, ask for help to run.
Press on. Paul's runner's word: chase hard toward the goal, the same verb he once used for persecuting, now aimed forward.
Your line: forgetting what's behind, reaching forth. The race isn't over yet. See you on the track tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Philippians 3:13–14 at new beginnings, such as a new year, a graduation or a recovery.

original.note: Greek: to chase, pursue, press on. Paul uses the same verb for persecuting the church in Philippians 3:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a motivational poster line.
what it means: Paul admits he hasn't arrived, lets the past stop steering, and runs toward the prize of God's calling.
what a scholar hears: diōkō, the verb Paul used for persecuting the church, now used for pressing on, and citizenship in heaven (3:20), picking up the citizen word of 1:27.
recall: asked Jesus to show them the Father

chat.says: Paul says forget what's behind. Does that mean pretending the past never happened?
options: No, he remembers it well; he just won't let it steer anymore. He runs forward.
Yes, he wiped his memory clean of everything he did before he believed.
No, he means look back often, so your old wins keep you motivated.
chat.meaning: Paul wrote his past down a few verses earlier, so forgetting isn't amnesia: the past no longer steers.

apprehended.meaning: old English for got hold of, grasped

the mark.meaning: the goal at the end of the track

Brethren.meaning: old English for brothers; here, fellow believers

Philippians.meaning: the believers in Philippi, a Roman colony

notes: Philippians 3:12 opens with a similar admission (not as though I had already attained); the quoted line is 3:13. Confirm.
διώκω in 3:6 (διώκων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν), 3:12 and 3:14: confirm.
πολίτευμα (3:20) as citizenship/commonwealth; KJV 'conversation' in its older sense of manner of life. Confirm gloss.
Philippi as a Roman colony: Acts 16:12. Athletic imagery is a standard reading of 3:13–14.
